title: Introduction to Deep Learning
subtitle: Contact session 1 · T1 Chapter 1 · what DL is, why now, and the four parts of every learning problem

lesson.title: What deep learning is
lesson.lead: Deep learning is machine learning with **many stacked layers** that learn increasingly meaningful representations of the data.

items: It is a subfield of machine learning built on artificial neural networks.
The **deep** refers to successive layers of representations. The number of layers is the model's **depth**.
Each layer extracts progressively higher-level features (pixels → edges → shapes → objects).
It learns by example, the way people do, instead of following hand-written rules.

Meaning

lesson.title: Why now?
lesson.lead: Deep learning took off because of **scale**: more data, cheaper compute and bigger networks.

items: Large amounts of unstructured data: images, text, audio, video.
Cheap, high-quality sensors and cheap storage.
Cheap computation: CPUs, **GPUs** and distributed clusters.
Automatic feature generation: no hand-crafted features.
Better learning ability and scalability.

blocks.label: Key picture
blocks.text: Andrew Ng's curve: with little labelled data, traditional ML (logistic regression, SVM) and neural networks perform similarly. As data grows, large neural networks keep improving while traditional algorithms plateau. **Scale drives deep learning progress.**

head: Amount of labelled data
What wins
rows: About a tie; depends on hand-engineered features
Large NN > medium NN > small NN > traditional ML

lesson.title: Applications and network types
lesson.lead: The input and output types decide the kind of network.

blocks.text: Other examples from the deck: weather forecasting from satellite images, question answering, outlining every person in a photo, and recommending products a user wouldn't otherwise find.

blocks.label: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: Match the network to the **input**: grids (images) → CNN, sequences (audio, text) → RNN, fixed-length tables → standard feed-forward NN.

lesson.title: The four core components
lesson.lead: Every deep learning problem has **data, a model, an objective function and a learning algorithm**.

items: **Data:** examples converted to numbers. Each example has **features** (covariates); in supervised learning it also has a **label** (target).
**Model:** the machinery that turns inputs into predictions, built from many chained transformations.
**Objective (loss) function:** measures how good or bad the model is. By convention **lower is better**.
**Learning algorithm:** searches for parameters that minimise the loss. The workhorse is **gradient descent**.

blocks.text: D = {X, t},   N = number of examples,   d = number of features (dimensions)
As the number of features grows, the **dimensionality** grows. A table of 8 houses with bedrooms, location, sq ft and price has N = 8 and d = 3 (price is the target).

blocks.label: Exam trap
blocks.text: Location is a word (Urban / Suburban / Rural), so it must be turned into numbers. Use **one-hot encoding** (Urban = [1,0,0], …), not 1/2/3, which would invent an order.

lesson.title: From program to model
lesson.lead: A **model** is a program whose behaviour is set by parameters that were learned from data.

items: Start with a program whose behaviour depends on parameters.
Use labelled examples to measure the loss.
**Train**: adjust the parameters to reduce the loss.
Once the parameters are fixed, the program is called a **model**.

blocks.text: The set of all programs you can get just by changing the parameters is a **family of models**. The same family should suit both "Alexa" and "Hey Siri" wake-word detection, because the tasks are similar.

blocks.label: Example from the deck
blocks.text: Wake-word example: collect lots of audio clips, label each as containing the wake word or not, and train a model whose output is yes or no.

lesson.title: Kinds of learning
lesson.lead: Supervised learning (this course) learns from **labelled** examples.

head: Kind
Data
Examples
rows: An agent acting in an environment over time

items: **Regression:** how much or how many? (price, temperature)
**Binary classification:** one of two classes (spam / not spam).
**Multi-class classification:** one of K > 2 classes (digit 0–9).
**Multi-label classification:** several labels at once (movie genres).
**Recommender systems**, and **sequence learning**: tagging, speech recognition, text-to-speech, machine translation.

lesson.title: Quick numbers to practise
lesson.lead: Mid-sem questions on this module are mostly counting: data shapes, splits, iterations and parameters.

blocks.text: iterations per epoch = ⌈N_train / B⌉        total updates = iterations × epochs
parameters of a Dense layer = inputs × units + units
Example: 12,500 clips split 80/10/10 → 10,000 train, 1,250 validation, 1,250 test. With batch size 64: ⌈10,000/64⌉ = 157 iterations per epoch; 15 epochs → 2,355 updates.

blocks.label: Preview
blocks.text: This playground shows what "learning algorithm" means: gradient descent walking down a loss bowl. Module 3 covers it in full.

worked.title: Data set shapes and one-hot encoding

problem.text: A table of 8 houses has columns ID, Bedrooms, Location (Urban / Suburban / Rural), Sq ft and Price. Price is the target. What are N and d? What is the design matrix shape if Location is one-hot encoded and ID is dropped?

steps.label: Raw d
steps.text: Features: bedrooms, location, sq ft, so **d = 3** (ID is not a feature, price is the target).

steps.label: One-hot
steps.text: Location becomes 3 columns: Urban [1,0,0], Suburban [0,1,0], Rural [0,0,1].

steps.label: Shape
steps.text: bedrooms (1) + location (3) + sq ft (1) = 5 columns, so X is **8 × 5** and t is 8 × 1.

worked.answer: N = 8, d = 3 raw features; X is 8 × 5 after one-hot encoding. One-hot avoids the false order that 1/2/3 would create.

worked.title: Splits, iterations and epochs

problem.text: 12,500 audio clips are split 80/10/10. Training uses batch size 64 for 15 epochs. How many iterations per epoch and how many weight updates in total?

worked.answer: 157 iterations per epoch; 2,355 updates in total. An epoch is one full pass over the training set.

worked.title: Counting parameters

problem.text: Count the trainable parameters of a fully connected 784 → 128 → 64 → 10 network.

worked.answer: 109,386 parameters (each layer: inputs × units + one bias per unit).

flashcards.back: ML based on neural networks with **multiple layers**, each extracting higher-level features from the data.
The number of successive layers of representation: the model's depth.
AI: machines doing human tasks. ML: learning from experience. DL: ML with layered neural networks.
